Library Administration Report 
August 2026 [covers our work for July] 
Snapshot of July:  
The busy, happy, super get -a-jump on reading spirit infused the library this month. Also 
influencing the library’s mood was the beginning of the fiscally challenging new budget year.  
 
Outwardly facing, staff engaged with the public with programs of all types [ i.e. The History of 
Sharks, superhero story time, Bubbleogy, making a hanging plant, grab and go’s, and a public 
reading by several of Hamden’s elected officials of the Declaration of Independence.] For more 
details and additional programs please read the full report. Summer reading itself is a program, 
spanning every age range with initiatives and prizes appropriate to each unique cohort. This 
year’s summer reading is extremely popular given that we printed 650 sign-up booklets and have 
had to make more! The circulation statistics are slightly up from last year and visits to the library, 
especially at Brundage, are increasing.  
 
Internally, we prepared to sustain  the 17% reduction in our library materials collection, staff 
worked with library vendors to seek reductions in prices for some of our digital services. 
Unfortunately, the library will no longer offer Ancestry . The CT State Library does offer a more 
localized version of Ancestry . By discontinuing our subscription, patrons lose access to national 
data. Fortunately, many vendors were willing to give us discounts and expressed their 
appreciation for the library. We are reducing Hoople checkouts to three a month due to the high 
cost of e-materials. 
 
Thus far the most challenging aspect of the reduced budget is staffing. Four library positions, 
including a part- time librarian position, are  frozen at $1. By itself that would be a tough but 
usually manageable problem to endure. However, since the beginning of July we have had 
multiple staff members out on medical leave. In some cases, these staff members have returned 
to work with abbreviated, shortened work schedules. Summer vacations and illnesses further 
shrunk the staff on several days. Alyssa Dansinghani’s skillful scheduling coupled with the staff’s 
willingness to take unmandated overtime and their flexibility to work multiple locations –  often 
in the same day – is what has kept the library doors open to the public. I don’t think we will always 
be so fortunate and there may well be times that a location could be closed due to lack of staffing. 
Please note that our overtime budget was reduced as well and by the third week of July we had 
already used 10% because of mentioned coverage issues.
2 
Extreme weather along with an attempted break-in at Brundage plagued the library system this 
month with water leakage, graffiti, a broken window, long grass, and overgrown “junk” trees in 
window wells. Miller’s failed HVAC system, even with the much appreciated workarounds, means 
that parts of the building are so warm that patrons opt not to work/sit there and staff work in 
offices as warm as 84 degrees. Poor public behavior, such as the vandalism and failed branch 
break in, have kept pace with the extremity of the weather. A particularly disturbing phone call 
put Miller on high alert. Sadly, we only anticipate more of the same.    
E
nding on a happy note, Library Journal honored the Hamden Public Library’s podcast, specifically 
our 2025 PRIDE episode, by naming it one of the notable government documents of 2025. This is 
a national honor. The podcast crew and guests who created this episode well deserve this special 
recognition. 
ADMINISTRATION 
Grants and Gifts 
• Open to You grant project, part of UCONN’s ReConnectCT – IMRP initiative, kicked off in  
earnest. The project’s goal is to normalize library usage for justice impacted and involved 
individuals. Mailers advertising the wide range of services were delivered to residences in 
the 06517 and 06514 zip codes. Almost a s soon as residents received these,  our offered 
computer classes filled up. Our newly hired digital naviga tors started helping clients  
through connections with Winning Ways and a re-entry house for women. Our drop-in legal 
database clinics have helped at least three people. Kimberly Leak’s expertise in social work 
has be en extremely beneficial with helping connect these services to the justice  
community. Likewise, Ryan McLaughlin of the Yale Opioid Substance Abuse Outreach Team 
has helped to connect folks to the program.
• READy for the Grade ran the whole month with average daily attendance of 14 rising first 
through third graders. This program is offered a t the Brundage branch,  a nd the ne wly 
reorganized design of the  branch was well received by these  emerging readers [and  
by everyone else, too!].
Staff 
• Working with Human Resources in Town, we are actively recruiting for two positions:
Branch Manager at Brundage and a part-time [15 hours a week] librarian.
• A
s previously mentioned, several staff members are in varying stages of medical leave.
Human Resources has been extremely helpful in developing solutions for abbreviated
schedules to meet these needs.
3 
 
• Alyssa and Melissa went offsite for our annual library administration retreat. The 
emerging theme from the retreat centered on improving communication, internally and 
externally.  
Facilities 
• The Town painter refreshed the upper children’s room and repaired the wall where the 
railing had fallen out.  
• Town IT worked on the final implementation of the CEN community Wi-Fi grant and 
helped with several malfunctions of our equipment.  
• Public Works cared for lawns when weather and staffing permitted.  
• Public Works responded to a lock issue at Brundage and is working on removing the 
“tag” from Brundage.  
• We have several projects needing their attention and while we understand that all Town 
departments need improvement, it would be helpful to have a bimonthly meeting with 
Public Works to go over library needs as we do have three locations to keep safe and 
sound.  
Outreach 
• Kimberly Leak, the digital navigators, and Melissa have reached out and connected with 
justice impacted organizations.  
• Melissa was a presenter at the Hamden Small Business Academy. 
• Melissa worked with the CT State Library in brainstorming on how to prepare libraries to 
receive laptops from DEEP.  
• Melissa represented the library system at the Town Center Master Planning community 
event.  
Associate Library Director’s Report by Alyssa Dansinghani 
The ongoing project at Brundage has concluded. Alyssa, Marcy and Kelly spent one last day 
finishing up the categorization of the picture books and got a head start on the labeling and 
“color coding” the final group of books. Kelly and her team have finished the final parts of the 
project and have put the books by category in our picture book bins.  
 
In addition to the day to day tasks and responsibilities, the month of July was spent working on 
the scheduling issues. At this time we have two staff on extended leave and two with altered 
schedules. As we are in the process of recruiting for two positions and multiple positions are 
frozen it has been nearly impossible to just keep the doors open. We have multiple staff 
working multiple branches, sometimes in one day, and multiple staff who are altering their 
schedules to assist with keeping the libraries open.

Snapshot of July:  
The busy, happy, super get -a-jump on reading spirit infused the library this month. Also 
influencing the library’s mood was the beginning of the fiscally challenging new budget year.  
 
Outwardly facing, staff engaged with the public with programs of all types [ i.e. The History of 
Sharks, superhero story time, Bubbleogy, making a hanging plant, grab and go’s, and a public 
reading by several of Hamden’s elected officials of the Declaration of Independence.] For more 
details and additional programs please read the full report. Summer reading itself is a program, 
spanning every age range with initiatives and prizes appropriate to each unique cohort. This 
year’s summer reading is extremely popular given that we printed 650 sign-up booklets and have 
had to make more! The circulation statistics are slightly up from last year and visits to the library, 
especially at Brundage, are increasing.  
 
Internally, we prepared to sustain  the 17% reduction in our library materials collection, staff 
worked with library vendors to seek reductions in prices for some of our digital services. 
Unfortunately, the library will no longer offer Ancestry . The CT State Library does offer a more 
localized version of Ancestry . By discontinuing our subscription, patrons lose access to national 
data. Fortunately, many vendors were willing to give us discounts and expressed their 
appreciation for the library. We are reducing Hoople checkouts to three a month due to the high 
cost of e-materials. 
 
Thus far the most challenging aspect of the reduced budget is staffing. Four library positions, 
including a part- time librarian position, are  frozen at $1. By itself that would be a tough but 
usually manageable problem to endure. However, since the beginning of July we have had 
multiple staff members out on medical leave. In some cases, these staff members have returned 
to work with abbreviated, shortened work schedules. Summer vacations and illnesses further 
shrunk the staff on several days. Alyssa Dansinghani’s skillful scheduling coupled with the staff’s 
willingness to take unmandated overtime and their flexibility to work multiple locations –  often 
in the same day – is what has kept the library doors open to the public. I don’t think we will always 
be so fortunate and there may well be times that a location could be closed due to lack of staffing. 
Please note that our overtime budget was reduced as well and by the third week of July we had 
already used 10% because of mentioned coverage issues.
